direction.comments: The macroscale has this indie surrealist feel that builds a fever-dream surrealist world, like a Charlie Kaufman movie but even more indie and even more gay; The microscale is very over-the-top campy with campy dialogue and character building, which is intentional, and has this hangout movie vibe like Dazed and Confused; The storytelling is basically non-existent because there really is no story or plot, as it is a hangout movie where plotlines converge at an end-of-movie party (like Dazed and Confused); The tension during the heavier, darker moments is definitely very high and makes you feel uneasy with what you are seeing on screen, but the campier moments are just so 90s corny that you cannot take the movie seriously in these moments

cast.comments: The cast is surprisingly stacked with a lot of big names for a low-budget indie queer movie; all the performances really are super over-the-top campy, averaging out to pretty bad with some parts being incredibly too campy, though some performances and moments are decent; because of how 90s camp the movie is, the chemistry feels incredibly forced and corny overall

story.comments: The concept is very much a microscope into the lives of 90s queer counterculture in LA on the West Coast, highlighting that lifestyle as if Kids had been shot on the West Coast; The movie also feels as if Dazed and Confused were set in the 90s and in Hollywood; The plot structure has basically no plot at all, operating as a hangout movie where plotlines converge at a party at the end (similar to Dazed and Confused), but they do not really do anything at that party; Despite my not being a huge fan of how over-the-top 90s campy and corny these characters are, you cannot deny the character writing serves as a vehicle to highlight the queer counterculture of the 90s, as each character represents a different aspect of it

screenplay.comments: The dialogue is the most 90s teenage dialogue ever and hurts to listen to, feeling like those low-budget middle school health class anti-drug videos from the 90s; The humor is incredibly over-the-top campy and 90s corny; The symbolism is surprisingly strong, touching deeply on 90s queer counterculture, angst, and relationships (especially with elements like the alien); The foreshadowing is virtually non-existent since there is really no overarching story or plot

soundtrack.comments: It is heavily driven by counterculture punk and power pop music; It barely felt like there was a score, as the movie relied much more on the 90s soundtrack

cinematography.comments: It uses a lot of wide-angle lenses that feel very 90s; While dated, it was still enjoyable, as it very much helped make the movie feel like a time capsule of 90s counterculture

editing.comments: The editing is very indie; There were many obvious moments where you could tell they had to chop something up or do editing flips in post-production to try to fix a scene

sound.comments: It has a very low-budget indie sound design overall, which works fine for what it is

visual_effects.comments: The movie has very low-budget indie visual effects, which work fine for what this movie is

production_design.comments: It is surprisingly good, as it creates a low-budget indie surrealist environment that contributes to the fever-dream feel this movie is going for

costumes.comments: The costumes help dress these characters as representatives of 90s counterculture and the lifestyle they live

review.pacing: The pacing feels incredibly slow and drags on significantly because there really is no underlying plot or storyline driving things forward
review.climax: The climax converges the multiple storylines at an end-of-movie party similar to Dazed and Confused, but it ends up playing out as a very over-the-top campy climax where nothing much really happens
review.tone: The tone very much feels as if Dazed and Confused were a movie about 90s teen, queer counterculture, as it is a hangout movie that explores different aspects of the lifestyle, mixing in surrealist and sci-fi elements to make this movie feel like a fever dream
review.overall: Overall, Gregg Araki's 'Nowhere' is an indie, surrealist fever dream that is the perfect time capsule of 90s teenage queer counterculture with its imagery, character writing, and campy, over-the-top dialogue; the only problem is that I hate the 90s, so this movie just really isn't for me
